content.p: On 7 April 1857, in the Sonoran town of Caborca, a former California state senator named Henry Alexander Crabb was tied by his raised hands to a post, with his back to a firing squad. A hundred or so bullets struck him, according to the account the San Diego Herald printed a few weeks later. A man then cut off his head with a knife, and the head was put in a jar of mescal. Around him, the men who had marched into Mexico with him had been shot in groups. Only a teenager lived.

The killings at Caborca, together with the deaths of four sick men on the American side of the border and of a second small party shortly afterwards, ended what the San Diego journal calls California's last and most notorious filibustering expedition to Mexico. For Americans the story was a massacre. For Mexican authorities it was the lawful end of an armed invasion. Both views have a long paper trail, and the tolls differ from source to source.

Crabb was born in Tennessee, trained as a lawyer and reached California in 1849, one of the thousands drawn by the gold discoveries. He went into politics, sat in the state senate and lost his bid for re-election in 1854. The San Diego Historical Society's journal adds that he was a Know-Nothing candidate for the US Senate in 1856 and lost again. He had also asked to join William Walker, a boyhood acquaintance, in Nicaragua in 1855, and been turned down.

Marriage tied him to Sonora. He married a daughter of the Ainsa family, prominent in both California and Sonora, which gave him contacts across the border. By the 1850s he was far from the only American with designs on Mexican territory. The journal names Walker, Morehead, Pindray and the Count de Raousset-Boulbon as earlier adventurers who tried to take parts of Sonora or Lower California in the first half of the 1850s. Crabb's attempt came as Mexico was still recovering from the loss of roughly half its territory in the previous two decades.

Sonora was divided. Two men were fighting for the governorship: Ignacio Pesqueira and the incumbent, Manuel María Gándara. A historian writing for Latin American Studies says Crabb told of visiting Sonora by ship in June 1855 with his brother-in-law Agustín Ainsa and talking to influential businessmen, who, Crabb claimed, were Pesqueira supporters and suggested he bring American colonists to settle the frontier and help control Indians. Gándara's partisans then accused Pesqueira of inviting the Americans, hoping the charge would turn Sonorans against him.

Whether Crabb and Pesqueira really struck a bargain is disputed. The San Diego journal says they supposedly agreed in 1856 that Crabb would supply military support in return for northern land, and that Pesqueira denied it once he had won control of the state without help. A magazine writer says that the revolutionaries agreed, though with a suspicion that Crabb intended to rule Sonora himself. Either way, Pesqueira was in power before Crabb left California, and the Americans he had been offered as allies were no longer wanted.

Crabb pressed on regardless. He recruited what he called the Gadsden or Arizona Colonization Company, almost 100 men by the journal's count, among them some wealthy and influential Californians according to the later historian. They sailed from San Francisco to Los Angeles in January 1857 and went overland by the southern emigrant trail. A small group under Robert N. Woods and Granville H. Oury went to Tucson to raise more men. Crabb had also arranged for General John D. Cosby to bring 900 recruits to meet him at Guaymas. They never came.

The Mexican government already knew of the plan. The historian writes that by 20 February 1857 it was well informed, and that John Forsyth, the US minister in Mexico City, had reported that newspapers there had carried rumours for weeks. On 26 March Crabb wrote from near Sonoita to José María Redondo, the prefect of Altar, calling the venture a legal colonising effort. Redondo did not answer. Pesqueira did, through a proclamation calling on Sonorans to fight what he called "this horde of pirates, without country, religion, or honor." A Mexican account summarised by the Flags of the World site, in which Agustín Aínza warned the governor of Crabb's plan, says that a party of 104 men crossed at Sonoita on 24 March and told the prefect that 900 more followers would join them.

Crabb took sixty-nine men toward Caborca and left about twenty to follow. The journal says he left his main ammunition supplies behind with the slower wagons. Accounts of the entry into the town differ. The 1857 report printed by the San Diego Herald says that a Mexican force commanded by Rodríguez met the Americans on 1 April and that, by hearsay, the Americans shot him dead as he came forward to talk. The journal summarises it the other way round: several Mexicans attacked, then fled when Crabb fired and killed their commander. The later historian says the defenders fired first on men walking through a wheat field.

The defenders fell back to the church on the plaza. According to the Herald report, Crabb's first and fatal mistake was not to rush it but to occupy houses on the corner of the plaza. More Mexican troops and volunteers arrived, and the Americans were hemmed in. The report says the Mexicans broke through the walls of neighbouring houses and set the buildings on fire more than once, and the Americans put the flames out. The Herald put the American dead at 25 over the fighting. Mexicans gave their own loss as 25 too, the report says, though it supposed the real figure much higher, as many as 200. That figure was an estimate by an unnamed informant, not a count.

The sources describe failed attempts to blow up the church. The later historian says that Crabb sent fifteen men with a keg of powder to its door and that the blast was too far away to break it, and that five of his men were killed doing it. The Herald report describes an attempt on the eighth day, with a keg under the portico, which killed the two men who tried it. Crabb was said to be wounded.

The balance was now far against him. The historian says that by 6 April more than 1,500 defenders with Papago allies had the building surrounded. A magazine account puts the Mexican force at about 1,200. On that day, according to the same historian, a flaming arrow fired by one of the Papago set the thatched roof alight. Crabb asked the Mexican commander, Hilario Gabilondo, for terms and was told, according to the historian, that the men would be treated as prisoners of war and given food and medical care. The Herald's informant said only that the Americans surrendered, "it is supposed unconditionally", and recorded that Crabb and fifty-eight men marched out under a white flag. The Mexican account has 59 filibusters giving up.

The prisoners were tied and held overnight in a corral. The historian says they got neither food nor medical attention. In the morning they were taken out in groups, in fives and tens according to the Herald report, and shot. The report says that the first volleys killed few outright because the executioners' aim was thrown by the prisoners' calm, and that the men were then turned to face away. Colonel W. H. H. McCoun was killed by a single ball at the first fire. Crabb was kept for last, questioned at the alcalde's office, allowed to write a letter to his wife and to see a captive doctor named Evans. The informant said Crabb "died as a gentleman should".

How many died that morning is not agreed. The True West writer says estimates run between 50 and 60. The California archive's finding aid describes 84 men leading the raid and two surviving, Jesus Ainsa and Charles Edward Evans. But Ainsa, according to a separate account in the journal, was arrested elsewhere, near Sonoita, and taken back to Sonora, and the Herald report said two of the Ainsa family were reported killed. The sources do not reconcile these.

The sole survivor of the main party, Evans, was 16 in the journal and 14 in True West; the Herald informant guessed 16 or 17. The magazine says that when Pesqueira ordered the prisoners shot, one commander refused, left and took the boy with him. The Herald informant did not know the boy's name and said only that the youngest was spared by the Mexican commander.

The aftermath of the shooting became part of the story Americans told. The historian says that, according to the survivor, Mexicans boasted that their hogs fed on the bodies. The San Diego journal says the bodies lay unburied outside the cemetery wall, and that the head was exposed to a jeering crowd.
content.h2: Tucson, Sonoita and the second party
content.p: Two other groups were caught up. The Tucson Valley Company, 26 men according to the journal and about 30 according to the Herald report, set out for Caborca under Wood and Oury. According to the journal, it could neither reach Crabb nor help him. The party's own statement, printed in the Herald, says that a Mexican force of 300 to 500 told it to lay down its arms and be escorted out; the Americans instead fought through, learned that Crabb was surrounded, and retreated north with a running fight that cost a few lives on each side. Wood and Oury got their men back across the line.

Four sick men left behind at Sonoita had crossed to a house owned by E. E. Dunbar on the American side of the border. The Herald printed a letter from Captain William J. Ankrim, writing from Fort Yuma, who said he was at Sonoita when it happened. A detachment of 25 Mexican soldiers took the men prisoner on the night of 17 April, he said, and shot them at dawn. Papago people buried the bodies. Ankrim added that Dunbar had for six or eight months sold goods from the house without interference from Mexican authorities, which he offered as evidence that the house was beyond Mexican jurisdiction.

A fourth group, about sixteen men under Freeman S. McKinney who were following with the ammunition, was found by a Mexican patrol a few days after the executions, according to the journal. The San Diego Herald reported on 6 June that they surrendered and were shot.

The first report of the disaster appeared in the San Diego Herald on 2 May 1857, based on travellers who reached the border town, and a fuller version followed on 9 May. San Francisco's Alta California and the Sacramento Daily Union reprinted it on 14 May. The Alta California never questioned it. The Sacramento paper doubted the more lurid details and, two days later, judged the earlier account the more reasonable. The Los Angeles Spanish-language paper El Clamor Publico carried a translation on 16 May and challenged the Herald's bias. The journal says the New York Times simply reported that Crabb and his party were shot.

The journal's author warns that the Herald should be read with care. Its editor, John Judson Ames, had backed taking more Mexican land since 1851 and made no secret of his sympathy with filibusters and his contempt for Mexicans.

On 30 May 1857 Forsyth told Mexico's foreign minister that the execution of Crabb and his party was "unmitigated murder", and described them as innocent immigrants with family ties in Mexico. Mexico replied that they had come into the country as an armed group without permission, that it was a filibustering expedition, and that Mexican law required the invaders to be executed. It offered no apology. Authorities in California advised Washington that Crabb appeared to have broken Mexican law, and the United States let the matter lie.

The journal's author says the minister did protest the execution of the party without a fair trial, but that Washington thought it better not to press even the deaths of the four men near Sonoita, since Crabb's men had crossed the border after being told to stay out. The True West writer says the episode could have turned into another war between the two countries, but neither government wanted one, and after the first outrage the expedition was forgotten.

The historical writing cited here stresses its significance. The journal calls it the most sensational and widely publicised of the American attempts on Mexican territory and says it closed nearly a decade of filibustering, a pastime that lost its glamour as the Civil War approached. The later historian argues that Mexicans meant to show Americans that such ventures could be fatal, and says no other American filibusters tried to enter Mexico during the rest of the 1850s.

A flag said to have been captured at Caborca on 6 April 1857 is held at the Museo Nacional de Historia at Chapultepec Castle in Mexico City. According to the Flags of the World site, it carries the words "Westward ho!!" on its canton.
